strengths: Strong theoretical contributions: NP-hardness result (Theorem 3) via clever Hamiltonian path reduction, and elegant characterization of incentive-compatible mechanisms (Theorem 6)
Novel problem formulation: First to systematically study tokenization misreporting as a principal-agent problem in LLMs, with clear economic motivation
Rigorous experimental methodology: Proper confidence intervals from 5 independent runs, multiple models and settings, transparent reporting of details
Clear presentation: Well-written with excellent motivating examples and figures (Figure 1 effectively shows tokenization distribution); honest limitations discussion
Comprehensive framework: Combines theory (proofs), algorithms (Algorithm 1), and experiments in coherent narrative addressing multiple aspects of the problem
weaknesses: Limited practical impact: Maximum overcharging only ~13% under optimal conditions (often <2%), and Algorithm 1 only succeeds in 30-100% of cases depending on settings; effectiveness degrades significantly at realistic temperatures (Figure 4 shows near-zero gains at temp 1.15)

Severely restricted experimental scope: Only 400 English prompts from LMSYS (acknowledged as potentially unrepresentative); character lengths restricted to [20,100]; critically, only open-source models tested—proprietary models (GPT-4, Claude) that dominate pricing not evaluated

Strong unvalidated assumption about transparency: NP-hardness result assumes providers commit to revealing next-token distributions—not verified for real providers; no exploration of why providers would voluntarily expose this information

Incomplete threat model: Doesn't address reputation/legal costs of misreporting, detection via multiple sampling, or why Algorithm 1 would be deployed in practice despite modest gains relative to discovery risk

Algorithm 1 concerns: Greedy token-splitting strategy lacks theoretical justification; only effective for temperature >1.0 (primarily creative writing); success rates in Figure 3 surprisingly low; no comparison to alternative approaches

Pay-per-character mechanism limitations: Proposed solution is not novel; creates inverse incentive for verbose outputs; speculation that it improves tokenization algorithms; implementation costs not discussed
Narrow scope: Focuses only on tokenization misreporting; ignores other provider mischiefs (model substitution, quality manipulation); doesn't explore hybrid pricing or multi-objective mechanisms

Generalization concerns: Limited to LMSYS dataset (which has been criticized [54,55]); character length range [20,100] may not be representative; only 5 runs for confidence intervals; unclear how findings extend to proprietary models or other domains

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Identifies genuine but understudied vulnerability in LLM-as-a-service pricing arising from information asymmetry and non-unique tokenization.
Sound theoretical contributions: Theorem 3 (NP-hardness via Hamiltonian path reduction) and Theorem 6 (characterization of IC mechanisms) are technically correct and provide useful insights.
Well-structured principal-agent model: Clearly formalizes the interaction between provider and user with appropriate economic framework.
Comprehensive theoretical analysis: Extensions of hardness results to top-k and probability-threshold settings strengthen the core contribution.
Proper experimental methodology: Includes confidence intervals, multiple model families, careful statistical handling of results.
Transparent limitations discussion: Honestly acknowledges scope constraints and broader impact concerns.
weaknesses: Limited practical threat magnitude: Maximum demonstrated overcharging is ~13% under unrealistic conditions (high temperature, p=0.99); drops to 0.3% under realistic parameters. Trivial character-tokenization attack (3-4×) would violate reported token probabilities and be immediately detected.

Evaluation scope too narrow: Tests only open-weights models (Llama, Gemma, Ministral), not proprietary APIs where threat is most relevant. Acknowledges but doesn't address that proprietary settings are the actual concern. Only 400 short LMSYS prompts, which authors note are criticized as unrepresentative.

Incomplete modeling of real constraints: (1) Assumes providers willingly share next-token distributions despite stating they are 'highly reluctant' to do so; (2) Linear cost model ignores KV-cache scaling and other nonlinear architectural costs; (3) Ignores reproducibility requirements that would add friction to attacks; (4) Doesn't model statistical detection via averaging across requests.

Proposed solution not deployable: Pay-per-character pricing requires external regulation rather than technical innovation. Oversimplifies by assuming uniform character cost (ignores UTF-8 encoding, special tokens, rare characters). No practical pathway for provider adoption. Transition strategy (rc = r₀/cpt) assumes unrealistic stability of character-per-token ratios.

Hardness result has limited practical implications: Theorem 3 proves worst-case NP-hardness but doesn't bound approximation quality on typical instances. The reduction specifically encodes Hamiltonian paths—doesn't characterize whether typical LLM outputs are easy or hard to manipulate. Gap between worst-case hardness and practice is unaddressed.

Algorithm 1 lacks principled analysis: Token-splitting heuristic is ad-hoc, motivated only by BPE structure. No ablations or comparison to alternatives. Heavy dependence on temperature—at temperature 1.0 (common in production), effectiveness is negligible. Efficiency claim relies on single plausibility check but doesn't address more sophisticated multi-step attacks.

Incomplete threat model: Doesn't analyze subtle manipulations that preserve top-p probabilities, biasing generation toward tokenizable outputs, whitespace padding, or intermediate-token attacks. These alternatives could be more practical than the proposed algorithm.

Presentation overclaims threat: Title and conclusion suggest systemic vulnerability, but evidence is highly parameter-dependent. The 3× character-tokenization attack isn't realistic with transparency; the 13% achievable attack requires non-standard deployment settings.

Missing evaluation of realistic scenarios: No actual testing against LLM API providers; no evidence this threat manifests in practice. No quantification of realistic revenue impact or real-world examples.
Broader impact statement is weak: Distinguishes algorithm from adversarial ML 'proof-of-concepts' but doesn't engage with risk/benefit of publication without practical defenses.

strengths: Novel problem identification: Identifies a genuine but previously unexplored vulnerability in pay-per-token pricing mechanisms due to information asymmetry in LLM-as-a-service platforms

Strong theoretical contributions: NP-Hardness result (Theorem 3) is technically sound with clever Hamiltonian path reduction; characterization of incentive-compatible mechanisms (Theorem 6) is elegant and complete
Theory-practice bridge: Goes beyond proving hardness to demonstrate practical misreporting via Algorithm 1, showing the gap between worst-case theory and realistic exploitation
Comprehensive experiments: Tests multiple modern LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Ministral) with careful parameter sensitivity analysis, proper confidence intervals, and concrete examples of misreporting
Principled solution: Proposes pay-per-character as provably incentive-compatible mechanism with clear mathematical justification and potential positive externalities
Excellent presentation: Clear writing with effective motivation (San Diego example), informative visualizations, and thorough discussion of limitations and broader impact
weaknesses: Unclear practical threat: No evidence providers actually exploit this vulnerability; threat requires specific conditions (temp >1.0, high top-p); overcharging diminishes to <0.3% at default temperature=1.0; Algorithm 1 succeeds only on subset of outputs (40-80% in favorable cases)

Apparent contradiction in threat model: Algorithm requires providers to be transparent about next-token distributions while dishonestly misreporting—unclear why providers would voluntarily share distribution information if planning to misreport; limited exploration of user-side detection via local tokenizers

Implementation gap for proposed solution: Pay-per-character mechanism requires regulatory intervention with no adoption pathway; authors acknowledge it needs external regulation; backward compatibility issues with existing APIs not addressed; assumes uniform character pricing

Limited evaluation scope: Only open-weight models tested (proprietary models like GPT-4, Claude dominate market); LMSYS prompts may not be representative (acknowledged by authors); English-only evaluation; no quantitative analysis of actual real-world temperature/top-p usage patterns

Theoretical result limitations: NP-Hardness characterizes worst-case complexity but not average-case difficulty on realistic LLM distributions; linear cost model is simplified; principal-agent framework doesn't capture competitive dynamics or regulatory environment

Algorithm 1 design gaps: Token splitting strategy motivated by BPE heuristic but not systematically compared to alternatives; no ablation studies; no comparison with optimal solutions or upper bounds on achievable overcharging

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a real vulnerability in current LLM pricing mechanisms used by major providers
Strong theoretical contributions: NP-hardness result (Theorem 3) with sound Hamiltonian path reduction, and elegant characterization of incentive-compatible mechanisms (Theorem 6)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral) with proper statistical rigor (confidence intervals, repeated runs, energy measurements)
Clear presentation with effective motivation (Damascus example), precise mathematical notation, and honest discussion of limitations
Constructive solution with practical recipe for providers to transition to pay-per-character while maintaining average profit margins
Theoretical characterization of incentive-compatible mechanisms has independent interest beyond LLMs in mechanism design
weaknesses: Limited practical impact: overcharging is only 1–11% under viable conditions, <0.5% for common low-temperature settings (factual/code tasks); threat model narrower than introduction suggests

Restrictive conditions for profitable misreporting: requires provider transparency (which may be refused), high temperature (uncommon), and plausibility constraints; practical threat surface is modest
Theory-practice gap: NP-hardness of optimal misreporting undercut by simple greedy Algorithm 2 achieving near-optimal results; suggests hardness result may be loose or artifact of formulation

Pay-per-character solution has significant limitations: doesn't prevent verbosity attacks, reduces margins for non-English users (Figure 12), requires regulatory intervention, and doesn't address verbosity inflation

Incomplete evaluation: only open-source models tested (proprietary models unknown), LMSYS dataset may not represent real user distribution, no evaluation against providers with detection mechanisms, statistical auditing defenses only in footnote
Algorithm 2 is relatively straightforward greedy heuristic; limited exploration of alternative misreporting strategies or comparison to other approaches

Model assumptions not fully justified: linear cost scaling cgen(t)≈co·len(t) may not hold universally, single interaction model ignores repeated game dynamics, focus on additive mechanisms excludes other structures
Incomplete code availability (link incomplete in paper) and missing sensitivity analysis (e.g., why 600 prompts?)

strengths: Identifies a genuine information asymmetry problem in LLM-as-a-service pricing with clear real-world relevance
Rigorous theoretical analysis: Theorem 3 (NP-hardness via Hamiltonian path reduction) is correctly proven; Theorem 6 elegantly characterizes incentive-compatible mechanisms
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Llama, Gemma, Mistral) with proper statistical rigor and confidence intervals
Proposes a theoretically elegant solution (pay-per-character) with well-motivated incentive compatibility
Clear problem formulation and presentation; thoughtful discussion of limitations in Section 5
Provides concrete examples (Damascus) that effectively illustrate the core problem
weaknesses: Critical gap between theory and practice: NP-hardness proof for optimal tokenization doesn't explain why Algorithm 2 heuristic works so well, undermining urgency of hardness result

Practical threat is significantly overstated: with transparency, Algorithm 2 achieves only 0.28-11.2% overcharging (Figure 2) vs. 300% theoretical maximum; only viable at high temperatures in creative writing

Central transparency assumption is unrealistic: paper assumes providers voluntarily share next-token distributions, which proprietary model providers will refuse; circular logic that requires regulation stronger than the original problem

Proposed pay-per-character mechanism creates substantial new problems inadequately addressed: (1) 6-8% of outputs become unprofitable, (2) harms non-English users with lower margins (Figure 12), (3) doesn't prevent verbosity attacks, (4) makes profit margins unpredictable
Evaluation limited to open-weight models on LMSYS data which may not represent real usage; no testing on proprietary models; no user studies on whether pay-per-character would be adopted

Verification cost analysis incomplete: Table 1 shows per-output verification is 1.5-13x per-token generation cost, potentially making Algorithm 2 unviable for marginal outputs—undermines profitability claims
Overstated novelty: core insight (information asymmetry enables misreporting) is straightforward; principal-agent framework is textbook; NP-hardness for combinatorial problems is unsurprising
Incomplete mechanism design: dismisses transparency, trusted execution, statistical auditing, and competitive pressure without proper analysis; ignores alternative mechanisms from prior work [38,39]
Algorithm 2's heuristic (split tokens by index) lacks principled justification; no comparison to other heuristic strategies
Ethical concerns: provides working overcharging algorithm with code availability, dismissed too quickly by comparison to adversarial ML
Broader issues with solution: doesn't address market dynamics when providers use different schemes; doesn't explain why users haven't demanded defenses if problem is severe

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First systematic analysis of tokenization-based overcharging in LLM-as-a-service with clear practical relevance to industry economics

Strong theoretical contributions: NP-hardness result (Theorem 3) via elegant Hamiltonian path reduction establishes genuine computational barrier; complete characterization of incentive-compatible mechanisms (Theorem 6)
Effective theory-practice bridge: Algorithm 2 demonstrates that computational hardness doesn't prevent practical exploitation; clear empirical demonstration of vulnerability (up to 11% overcharging)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral), systematic variation of hyperparameters, energy measurements validating assumptions, multilingual analysis, appropriate statistical rigor
Complete solution: Not just problem identification but concrete, implementable alternative with practical transition mechanism maintaining provider margins
Excellent presentation: Intuitive examples, clear logical flow, thoughtful acknowledgment of limitations, well-organized structure
weaknesses: Limited scope on deployed systems: Experiments only on open-weight models; proprietary LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini) that dominate practice are absent; LMSYS prompts acknowledged as potentially unrepresentative of real-world distributions

Practical deployment barriers inadequately addressed: Solution depends critically on provider transparency about next-token distributions, yet paper acknowledges provider reluctance; no realistic path to enforce adoption or overcome resistance; proprietary tokenizers released differently from internal ones undermines verification

Limited novelty in solution: Pay-per-character pricing is relatively straightforward given linear generation costs; Theorem 6 characterization is somewhat intuitive; margin preservation prescription is elementary arithmetic

Algorithm limitations: Algorithm 2 performance degrades significantly at lower temperatures/p values (Figures 2, 6); simple greedy heuristic lacks theoretical justification; no exploration of more sophisticated misreporting strategies; no equilibrium analysis of multiple misreporting providers

Assumption scope: Linear generation cost assumption holds empirically for specific hardware but may not generalize; contract theory framing assumes provider self-designs incentives (unrealistic); only addresses tokenization misreporting, not verbosity padding which pay-per-character doesn't prevent

Evaluation limitations: Energy measurements on A100 GPUs with KV caching may not generalize; statistical audit procedure mentioned but not formalized; language equity concerns with pay-per-character reducing margins for underrepresented languages
